newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh faces challenges over privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh faces challenges over privatisation.

text.p: Bangladesh's attempts to privatise struggling state industries have met with multiple challenges, including strong opposition from trade unions and lack of buyers, a senior government official said on Friday.
Successive Bangladeshi governments have insisted there is no alternative to handing over loss-making industries to the private sector.
But restive labour unions, most with potential political backing from opposition parties, have effectively delayed the process if not fully halted it.
On the government's side, it has yet to receive enough calls from prospective buyers.
"Some of the prospects want to use the land (for other businesses) but not to run the factory," one government official said.
The trade unions want jobs to be protected or else handsome financial pay-offs.
"We are facing strong opposition from trade unions over privatisation," said Kazi Fazlur Rahman, chief of the Bangladesh Administrative Reforms Commission.
"But we are still hopeful about the successful implementation of our mission. We have no alternatives," he told Reuters.
Rahman did not suggest any radical move to hand over the industries -- measures that might prompt a political crisis.
"Each and every country has faced similar opposition...we are learning (how to deal with it)," he said.
Bangladesh has been pushing the privatisation process since 1991 after Begum Khaleda Zia became prime minister.
Her successor, Sheikh Hasina, has sought to reinforced the process -- but with little success.
No transfer to the private sector occurred during Khaleda's five-year rule, and only one mill has been transferred since Hasina took office in June 1996.
The government's Privatisation Board has listed 95 state-owned enterprises (SOE) in jute, textile, engineering, sugar, food and chemicals sectors for disposal.
The government recently called for bids for 13 SOEs, and said it would sell its shares in 18 enterprises, chairman of the Board, Kazi Zafarullah, said.

Sramik Karmachari Oikya Parishad (SKOP), the umbrella body of the workers' federations in both public and private industries, called a general strike on July 29 in protest against the privatisation bid.

One SKOP leader told Reuters that "thousands of mills and factories had already been closed since 1991 and more than 20,000 of workers at state-owned companies had been sacked under the (privatisation) reform programme. So the process must be stopped".
S.A. Malek, political adviser to Hasina, said: "This (privatisation) is a major policy issue for the government since it had adopted free market policies."
Bangladesh has suffered losses of nearly $1.86 billion over the past five years due to the inefficient running of public enterprises, Zafarullah said.
But the government seems to lack the political will to carry the process through.
The SKOP has strong backing from Khaleda's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).
"This is quite contradictory on the part of BNP because they were a strong pusher of the privatisation process," said one government leader, who declined to be identified.
"The government has given 420 billion taka ($9.76 billion) in subsidy to state owned enterprises over the past 21 years," Zafarullah said.

"The SOEs were also given huge loans, but 90 percent of it, nearly 130 billion taka ($3.02 billion), has not been repaid. This has resulted in a severe liquidity crisis in the lending banks," he said.
